body: German speakers can catch the familiar word Wolf in the name, which in Dutch means the same thing - wolf. The whole name Wolvendaal means Wolf Valley. What do wolves have to do with it? Nothing to do with it. In the mid-18th century, this part of the Pettach area was outside the city walls, and the Dutch mistook bush-rummaging jackals for wolves, hence the name. The main Dutch church of Ceylon (of course already Protestant at the time) was built in 1749. In the equinox cross-shaped building, the Dutch buried their governors-general (in five numbers) until the Dutch East India Company was supplanted by the English. At the time of the visit, it was closed, but in the case of Protestant churches, this is not a big deal: the interior is rarely richer than the exterior...
title: What do wolves have to do with it?

body: Dutch era in Ceylon in the 17th century was marked by relative peace and increased trade, but that doesn't mean they were healthy. The church is a veritable fossil trove of past. Almost all Burgher families in Sri Lanka have at least one grave or crypt at this place; it's the Godric's Hollow for Burghers in Sri Lanka. Plus, the church itself was said to be haunted some time in the past, and the surrounding area is home to a lot of superstitious tales. If you're lucky to encounter an old Tuk Tuk driver, be sure to ask him.
title: Window into a Haunting Past

body: Perhaps the most interesting Colonial building in Colombo this exquisite Dutch church was completed in 1757. The building once sat in a swampy area known as the wolf's dale due to the mistaken belief that packs of roaming Jackals were in fact wolves. It now sits on a busy urban street in a commercial and residential area. The church needs some TLC but the fact that it has not been restored also gives it a very authentic feel. The Dutch Fort for example has been renovated to the point that it has no historic feeling. The exterior of the church shows the elegant 18th Century classical detail popular at the time and you can see lovely original details like the original escutcheon on the main door. In addition the church is flanked by numerous 18th Century Dutch tombstones and inside are more stones and plaques to deceased Dutch and English parishioners. Inside the church the pulpit, baptismal font, the choir gallery and the pews are all early carved wooden pieces. There are numerous early 19th Century English arm chairs from several different sets as well as early Dutch chairs. There are some spectacular box locks on the doors. The sparse white walls and the glass hanging lamps give the interior a very 18th Century Dutch appearance. There is also an interesting 19th Century pipe organ. I met a Dutch Australian Family searching out their family history while I was at the church. For those interested in Colonial history this church is not to be missed.
title: Really Spectacular

body: Tucked away in the old city part of Colombo this Dutch Reformed Church was built in 1749 by the Dutch East India Company. It has weathered life in Colombo for all of these years and there are interesting points to see both inside and outside the church building. Of particular note are the gravestones of the Dutch settlers and colonists who died in this country and were buried on site. Remnants of the British period of occupation can also be seen in and around the church, and these stand in stark contrast to those of the Dutch period. The caretaker on site can provide a very interesting and detailed account of the history of the church and the city, and I encourage you to listen to his narration. Donations towards the upkeep of the church are requested but not demanded. 100 LKR is a good starting point but we thought 500 was more appropriate. Well worth a visit. Highly recommended.

body: The Wolvendaal Church was built by the Dutch Reformed Church with assistance of VOC Company in 1749. When the church was built, this area was a wild area beyond the city walls. The Dutch mistook the packs of roaming jackals for wolves, and the area became known as Wolf’s Dale, or Wolvendaal in Dutch. The church, whose foundations were laid in 1749, took 8 years to build and is capable of seating 1000 persons. Completed on 6th of March 1757, it was dedicated for public worship by Rev. Matthias Wirmelskircher, Rector of the Colombo Seminary. The church was constructed in the Doric style of the period, in the form of a Greek cross, with walls nearly five feet thick, over which the gables have been raised. The dome was originally arched with brick and surmounted with a brazen lion. This lion had a crown on its head, bearing a sword in one hand and seven arrows in the other, representing the seven united provinces of the Dutch Republic. In 1856, a bolt of lightning destroyed this lion and seriously damaged the dome. The roof was later replaced with an iron covering. The real treasure is its Dutch furniture. The Dutch governors had a special pew made with elegant carved ebony chairs. The wooden pulpit, ebony and calamander chairs, baptismal font and lectern all belong to the Dutch era. The floor is paved with tombstones of those who lie buried within the church. One can find many famous names of 300 year Sri Lankan history: Dutch, Burgher, Singhalese, Tamil and English.
title: Must visit Dutch period church

body: Sandwiched in the middle of the busy Pettah district sits the historical Wolvendaal church. It's not that easy to find unless your Tuk Tuk driver drives you (or you've got a really good map of the area). It is a quiet reflective oasis in this part of town. The oldest church in Colombo (3rd oldest in Sri Lanka) - is still a working church and because its a Dutch Protestant church its not an ornate tourist attraction however it is steeped in history. The church's verger/caretaker is knowledgable, patient and happy to show you around the church and the grounds and explain the building's quirky heritage. There are no fees as its a normal church however after having a guided tour and seeing that it is in need of repairs I was more than happy to make a donation to assist in its upkeep.
title: A peaceful piece of Colonial history

body: My girlfriend and I had a walk in the old trading district of Pettah when suddenly an (unwanted) guide appeared who took us along to the Wolvendaal Church. He arranged us some sort of tour with the museum/church conservator. The old man knew the history of the reformed church, the VOC and EIC and told us some interesting facts about the choir, barrel and the pulpit. Apparently the church is constructed in such a way that the ships entering the harbor had a clear view on the building. After the small tour the conservator asked us a small donation. Because the church desperately needs to be renovated, I prefer the one in Malaysian Melaka. But it is still one of the old heritage sites in the city, and if you’re a little bit familiar with European colonial history, you will enjoy this. Not at least becaues it gives you the opportunity to escape the heat for a few moments.

title: Old church with tinge of dutch architecture and settings

body: This church was built in the 18th century during the Dutch occupation of Ceylon. It is a wonderful example of Hollandic architecture and has tablets on the wall and is paved with the tombstones of ancient Dutch parishioners. The cordoned off section in which prisoners were brought in to participate in the worship is still there as are the original ebony pews and pulpit, which overlooks the congregation. at a high elevation.The approach is not so great, the church being in the heart of the Pettah, which is now the precinct of vendors but during the Dutch era, was a residential area of the elite.Well worth a visit.
title: Dutch period architechure

body: This remarkable church is certainly full of history. The balance of the reviews here are quite accurate so I won't repeat commentary on the content. And I agree, best to have a guide or let the caretaker take you around and tip accordingly. We went with Colombo City Walks and it just seemed like the perfect place to relax and take in some history after the Pettah Market.It reminds you that this island has had no shortage of landlords per se and it is nice to find something so well preserved from so long ago. The stained glass windows are from the British - and so within the last century more or less - but they replaced slates which are, of course, more traditionally Dutch - and not so secure. The combination is lovely.There were no other tourists at the time, so I took the opportunity to play the church piano - and while a little out of tune, the sounds of gospel bounding off the three foot thick walls was thrilling!
title: A lovely place to visit if you have been rushing around!

body: Built in 1749 by the Dutch East India company although the Dutch Reformed Chruch dates back to the 1640s. Perviosuly hand-pumped, now motorised pipe organ. Grave stones around the outer perimeter of the church as well as inside. Helpful gentleman provided a tour of the church. Rps100 is requested donation. Fans strewn around the church (not operating) along with projector and loud religious music being played on the day we visited. A pale comparison to the much more beautiful Dutch Reformed Church in Galle. For directions, see my review of 'Old Town Hall'.
title: Historical but uninspiring

body: Once set on a lot more land, the DRC at Wolvendaal is now "squeezed" into an odd shaped piece of land, traffic all around, that's progress i suppose. I visited on a very hot day (aren't they all in Colombo?) and it was some relief to go inside. Beautiful stained glass, headstones telling the history not only of the church, but Ceylon / Sri Lanka itself. Doesn't take long to get there, you don't have to spend oodles of time there, but well worth a visit. Photography is allowed, but be respectful, AND make sure you give a few Rs to help with up keep of the church please?
title: Wonderful Church

body: I've been to this church twice, once for a wedding and the second time with Colombo City Walks. This is a very interesting church with old photographs, eerie grave markers of those who died of disease and walled up secret tunnels. There isn't much in the way of interpretive material so you really need a guide to get the best out of a visit here.

body: The Dutch word Wolvendaal means the ‘Dale of Wolves’ and it relates to an area outside the Fort of Colombo in Sri Lanka which was in the 17th century covered with swamps and marshland. Animals identified as wolves (in fact they were jackals!) used to roam here unhindered. In the middle of this area, on a hill overlooking Colombo, stands the majestic Wolvendaal Church. Built in 1749, it is one of the oldest Protestant churches still in use on the island and considered one of the most beautiful and historically interesting churches of South Asia. very good place to visit.

body: I was surprised to know that they still hold services in this ancient church. Despite being over 250 years old there is door with an ancient lock that still functions! The caretaker took us on a tour of the church, it is quite an experience to view the ancient choir pews, the benches where the congregation sat, the pulpit and the pipe organ which is sadly not functional.

body: Had to visit the church for a assignment, and found a quaint church in the middle of pettah hidden by the busy hustle and bustle. The church dates back to the dutch period and caught me by suprise, the church is a dated but is kept in good condition. It still carries the old school church organ. I took many pictures and the brother present at the time was very helpful with the lighting. Probably the oldest dutch reformed church in Sri Lanka. Address is: Wolvendaal Lane Pettah, Col 11. Open from 9am-3.30pm

body: This church was recommended to us for a visit. There was no one else there and the admission "fee" was a miniscule donation. We took lots of pictures inside and out as it is a true oasis of calm and historical importance in this overly busy city. I sat in the pews and explored every area of the interior, trying to imagine the congregants sitting where I was, hundreds of years ago.

body: First of all, this church was pretty much unknown to our tuk tuk driver. He had to stop twice for directions, and we had no map on us to help. The locals know this as the "old Dutch church," and that seemed to help when we were asking for directions. It's next to the small green mosque.Anyway, once we found it, we felt like we'd stumbled upon an old historic secret. The building has seen better days, but the guy who gave us an impromptu tour was very informative and friendly (be sure to slip him a few hundred rupees for his trouble, as is the local custom). My husband and I both enjoyed our visit, though he was very dismayed at the state of disrepair the building was in. I thought the whole thing was pretty cool and would suggest you make the effort to stop by this cute old church with a really interesting story.

title: A must visit when in Pettah
body: Pettah is close to the Colombo Harbour, and the 1st place that most items arrive in Sri Lanka. A walk through Pettah is quite an experience, and you can get quite a few bargains. Wear light cotton clothes and closed shoes as it could get quite warm and dusty. The Wolvendaal Church has been built over 250 years ago and the oldest tomb stone is dated 1668! There is a tour guide on site or you could speak to the caretaker who has a wealth of knowledge. He could even read Dutch! It is a place you should spent at least 1 hour at.
